metadata.title: Gradient Descent on a Parabola
metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.objective: See why a descent step goes opposite the gradient and is scaled by the learning rate.
misconceptions: A larger learning rate is always better
expectedUnderstanding: the update is x minus eta times the local slope
slope f'(x) = 2x points uphill, so the step uses its negative
step length = eta times |slope|, so it shrinks near the minimum
a large eta can overshoot and zigzag

checkpoints.title: Start at x = 2.4
checkpoints.body: The curve is f(x) = x^2, so the slope at the point is f'(x) = 2x = 4.8, pointing uphill to the right. The arrow points the other way, downhill, because the update subtracts the gradient.

checkpoints.title: Step 1: scaled by eta
checkpoints.body: The step is delta x = -eta * f'(x). With eta = 0.3 that is -0.3 * 4.8 = -1.44, landing near x = 0.96. Push eta up and the arrow lengthens at the same point; push it down and the step shrinks.

checkpoints.title: Steps shrink near the bottom
checkpoints.body: At x close to 1 the slope is only about 1.9, so the next step is smaller even though eta has not changed. The step size multiplies eta by the current slope, so it shrinks as the point nears the minimum.

checkpoints.title: Try a large eta
checkpoints.body: Set eta to 0.9 and the first step jumps past the minimum to x about -1.92, then the next step jumps back across. Overshooting is why a bigger learning rate is not automatically better; here it zigzags instead of settling.

checkpoints.title: Why opposite the gradient
checkpoints.body: f'(x) = 2x points in the direction of steepest increase. To make f smaller you move along minus f'(x). At the minimum the slope is 0, so the step is 0 and the point stops: that is what convergence means in this scene.

narration.text: A point sits on the parabola; the arrow is one descent step from its current x.
Each step is the learning rate times the slope, aimed opposite the slope.
As the slope flattens near the minimum, the steps get shorter.
A large learning rate makes long steps that can cross the valley.

fallback.text: A point descends a parabola y = x^2 in three steps. At each step it moves horizontally by eta times the slope, in the direction opposite the slope, so it moves toward the minimum at x = 0. Steps get shorter as the slope flattens. A learning rate near 0.9 overshoots past the minimum and zigzags.

accessibility.alt: A parabola with a point on its right branch and a horizontal arrow pointing left toward the minimum; the arrow length and the point's position change with the learning-rate slider.
